Ground mismatch: LAC are run-first (40% pass when leading) into a ARI front that bleeds 128 rush yds/game and 0.47 RB1 rushing scores. Omarion Hampton is a centerpiece — and the game script only feeds him.

The LAC host the ARI as favorites of 11.5, with the total set at 45.5 — a market that implies a LAC 28–17 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 56% of its snaps with LAC in front, 26% within one score, and 18% with LAC chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

This projects as a game LAC should control. A favorite of 12 sits in front for the majority of the second half in most simulations, which pulls the script toward the run and clock management for LAC and toward volume passing and tempo for ARI, who will be throwing to keep pace. Expect ARI to run more total plays than LAC — trailing teams go no-huddle (league no-huddle rate climbs from ~8% in neutral game states to over 20% when down two scores), and that extra volume is a tailwind for ARI's pass-catchers even in a losing effort.

Touchdown Board

Oronde Gadsden II is a live anytime-TD dart — ARI are leaky to tight ends in the end zone (0.32 TE TDs/game vs ~0.24).

Ladd McConkey carries TD equity — ARI surrender 0.47 WR1 receiving scores a game.

In the red zone ARI throw it (59% pass inside the 20) — Michael Wilson's TD equity over a goal-line back.

Game Script, Pace & Environment

Script leans LAC. As a 12-point favorite they project to lead much of the game, tilting toward the run late — Omarion Hampton's carry ceiling rises in the blowout branches. Meanwhile ARI throw to keep pace, a volume tailwind for Michael Wilson.

Fade the ARI run — as 12-point dogs projected to chase, James Conner's carries get squeezed, though his receiving work ticks up in catch-up mode.

A middling 46 total — no strong lean either way; the value is in the individual matchups above, not the game environment.

Indoors — a dome removes weather variance and historically nudges passing efficiency up; a small tailwind for the passing games.

LAC — a run-heavy offense

LAC are one of the league's more run-committed offenses: on early downs while leading, they pass just 40% of the time, against a league average of 44% — a genuine clock-bleeding identity, not noise (it holds after shrinking their sample toward the league).

This is the profile that most rewards a lead back. As a 12-point favorite projected to lead for 56% of snaps, LAC will be running to close the game, and their run-first identity compounds it. Omarion Hampton is the beneficiary — we project 10 carries for 41 yards, and his ceiling is where the value sits: in the simulations where this becomes a two-score game, his volume spikes as LAC salt it away.

The flip side: Ladd McConkey (5 targets, 42 yards) has his ceiling capped by the same script that helps the run game — when LAC lead and run, there simply aren't as many pass attempts to go around. He's a safer floor than ceiling play in this spot.

Underneath, Oronde Gadsden II (TE, 3 targets, 31 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

ARI — a balanced offense

ARI are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (45% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

Game script works against the run here — ARI project to trail and throw, which squeezes James Conner's rushing projection (10 carries, 46 yards) but raises his value as a receiver; trailing teams check the ball down, and his target share ticks up as the game gets away from them.

Michael Wilson is the one to target from a volume standpoint: as underdogs throwing to keep pace, ARI funnel work to their top receiver — 8 targets for 70 yards projected, with genuine upside if they fall behind early and the game turns one-dimensional.

Underneath, Trey McBride (TE, 11 targets, 85 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 12-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.

This preview and the projections below regenerate through the week as injuries, weather and line moves update the inputs.
